ground_truth:
Final confirmed diagnosis: Urinary bladder paraganglioma (functional/catecholamine-secreting extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma of the bladder wall). The presentation mimicked a far more common condition — it was initially diagnosed and treated as an anxiety disorder (SSRI prescribed) and later labeled "migraine with generalized anxiety disorder." The key clue was that the adrenergic spells (palpitations, diaphoresis, headache, weakness, nausea) were temporally tied to micturition — voiding mechanically squeezes the bladder-wall tumor and triggers catecholamine release.

How confirmed: Histopathology of the resected mass showed the classic Zellballen pattern (nests of chief cells separated by fibrovascular septa) with vesicular chromatin and eosinophilic granular cytoplasm; immunohistochemistry positive for chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and CD56, with low Ki-67 (~1%), confirming a paraganglioma. An intraoperative hypertensive crisis (BP rose to 170/100 mmHg after induction, managed with glyceryl trinitrate) on manipulating the tumor further supported a catecholamine-secreting lesion.

Correct disposition/treatment: Recognize the catecholamine-secreting nature pre-operatively; ideally biochemical workup (plasma/urinary metanephrines, VMA) and alpha-blockade before resection to avoid intraoperative hypertensive crisis. Definitive treatment was surgical excision (partial cystectomy)
judge_rationale:
GROUND TRUTH: Urinary bladder paraganglioma (functional catecholamine-secreting extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma), initially misdiagnosed as anxiety/migraine; key clue = micturition-triggered adrenergic spells; confirmed by histology (Zellballen, chromogranin A/synaptophysin/CD56+, low Ki-67) plus intraoperative hypertensive crisis on manipulation; correct disposition = pre-op recognition, biochemical workup (metanephrines/VMA) + alpha-blockade before surgical excision (partial cystectomy), then post-op surveillance.

CORE DIAGNOSIS: Both outputs nail the primary diagnosis (bladder paraganglioma / catecholamine-secreting pheochromocytoma) and the central mechanistic insight — micturition mechanically squeezes the bladder-wall tumor, releasing a catecholamine bolus. Both correctly identify the anxiety misdiagnosis as the trap, correctly read the intraoperative hypertensive surge as the catecholamine signature, and both recommend the right confirmatory/safety step: biochemical metanephrines + alpha-blockade before resection. On the core verdict they are essentially tied and both correct.

OUTPUT A (structured/probabilistic): Strengths — explicit ranked posteriors, correctly demotes urothelial carcinoma (the tempting "bladder mass" distractor) and panic disorder, fires the right discriminators (absent hematuria against urothelial Ca, post-void trigger, intraop crisis). It correctly names histology/immunostains (chromogranin/synaptophysin) as an open confirmatory item, matching ground truth. Calibration framing (VOI, decision threshold, "no kickback") is internally coherent. Weak
